title: Crown Estate Admits Veeraswamy Eviction Plan Is Purely Financial as Trial Ends
excerpt: At the close of a five-day trial, the landlord told the court the Regent Street restaurant's space would be far more valuable as offices. Judgment in the case of Britain's oldest Indian restaurant is expected before the end of the year.
body:
• Veeraswamy, the Michelin-starred restaurant that has traded in Victory House on Regent Street since 1926, will close if it loses its court fight with its landlord, the Crown Estate, its owner told The Times.
  • Closing the five-day trial at Central London County Court on Wednesday, the Crown Estate's barrister said the reasons for turning the restaurant's floors into offices were purely "financial."
  • The Crown Estate has already done soft strip-out work on the building's office floors and aims to sign the main works contract by early January and start the main works by next March, the court heard.
  • Judgment is expected before the end of the year. The restaurant remains open and trading while the case is decided.

It would be a "tragedy" to force Britain's oldest Indian restaurant to close, its owner said, as its landlord admitted in court that the plan to replace it with offices is purely financial. The exchange came at the end of a five-day trial at Central London County Court, where Veeraswamy's owner, MW Eat, is resisting the Crown Estate's attempt to end its tenancy at Victory House, near Piccadilly Circus.

What the landlord told the court

Mark Sefton KC, representing the Crown Estate — which manages King Charles's property portfolio — told Judge Alan Johns KC that the estate took the view that "the space occupied by the restaurant will be far more valuable if redeveloped into high-class office accommodation than if it remains in restaurant use." He said the landlord recognised the heritage and cultural value of the restaurant, but that the financial return of the office scheme was "incredibly compelling," and that it had spent several years and several million pounds developing the project, obtaining planning and listed-building consent. The conversion is part of a wider £1 billion regeneration scheme for the area.

The restaurant's case

MW Eat, which has owned Veeraswamy since 1996, is seeking a new tenancy under the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954. Its barrister, Guy Fetherstonhaugh KC, told the court the landlord's plans involved evicting the restaurant but not the nightclub and retail unit on the building's ground and basement floors, and that the premises were "very much not old and worn or ripe for redevelopment." He argued the landlord simply did not wish its planned offices to have an Indian restaurant among them, however prestigious. Sefton disputed that, arguing the building's office entrance is too small for prime West End office space and that the restaurant entrance would cease to exist once the works are carried out. MW Eat has put the cost of relocating at up to £5 million, as London Daily News reported.

"We fought because we want to keep the restaurant open."

— Ranjit Mathrani, chairman of MW Eat

A century on Regent Street

Veeraswamy was founded in 1926 by Edward Palmer, great-grandson of General William Palmer, secretary to the first governor-general of India, and the Moghul princess Faisan Nissa Begum. It is one of the oldest occupants of Regent Street and has served diners including Princess Anne, Charlie Chaplin and Mahatma Gandhi. Its lease, reported at £205,000 a year, expired in June 2025. In February, a petition with more than 20,000 signatures was delivered to Buckingham Palace asking the King to intervene.

Ranjit Mathrani, chairman of MW Eat, told The Times that closure "would be a tragedy, not just for the loss of a major historic venue which has contributed so much to British culinary history and London and Regent Street, but also a loss to ourselves." Judgment is expected before the end of the year. Until then, the restaurant continues to trade at Victory House.
